chapter: On the road with the Moores
title: How the Moores' drunk-husband routine played
summary: Green and the interviewers talk through the satirical routine of the husband who comes home tight with fictitious employers, singing I'm Busted.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: This was, I guess, hilarious to
the audience, of course.
Yes, tremendous comedy, really was.
So there was a whole dramatic structure to it, of him trying to find a job and her scolding him each time that he didn't get a job?
Satirical --
Right. Right. He had to explain why he didn't get no work or something, you know.
Uh-huh. And it all revolved also around the illegal act of going and get liquor. It was illegal. You weren't supposed to do that.
Yeah, he been to the bootlegger's, yeah.
(Laughter)
Okay. Do you remember any of those particular lines that they used to have or those particular jokes?

Yeah, well, that's what I'm saying. I mean the comical part of it was when he would mention some fictitious employer, some name, you know, but he's trying to tell his wife that -- how important this employer is, and he's Mr. Big, you know. Very important man, That employer, lot of money and this, that and the other thing and she would say to him, 'Well, it's funny you never -- when you come back in, you haven't given me nothing, and he -- and he would go into another song, you know, about 'I'm Busted', you know.

Other words, he let the cat out of the bag by explaining that he don't have no money, you understand. See, sometimes he would say, well, I worked at the end of my first four hours or something, you know, and she would say, well, what about the pay, you know, and he would go into his song, you see -- I'm Busted.

So now that's -- see, but he would always -- his bottle would be empty, you know, and he'd have a corner in it, and he would hide it under the back porch steps, you know, then and he'd go up the steps, and he'd do some comedy going up the steps, you know, like staggering and so forth, and he'd knock on the door -- whack, wack, wack, wack, wack.

And the door would fly open -- bam -- and there she's standing there with the black face, you know, and big eyes, 'It's you; what took you so long?' You know. And she start -- he started to backing back down the steps, you know.
(Laughter)
You understand? You get the picture?
So but -- (RECORDING INTERRUPTION)
(Inaudible) important line.

Yeah, you see, that was a way of life, you see. It was actually a reality because these bootleggers, the law was after them, you see, what they call the revenooers or something, you see. And Mr. Moore, Chinch Moore, you see, they based their routines on these realities of life, ways of
life, you see. And that's what made it so comical, because -- pardon me, please.
(Inaudible).
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
